notes: Gear catalog for Olympic Peninsula Hiker (design data, 2026-10). UNITS: weight_oz is ounces (16 oz = 1 lb; 1 L of water = 35.2 oz). volume_l is packed liters: stuffed size for soft goods, OUTSIDE size for rigid items (canisters, pots), and for 'worn' items the volume they take if carried instead. price_usd is the 2026 shelf price at an ordinary outfitter, before any in-game store multiplier (the last-chance store on the drive can mark up). CARRY: 'inside' must ride inside the pack; 'outside_strappable' may go inside or on an outside strap, tool loop or side pocket (outside = exposed to rain and snags, simulation.md 6.3); 'worn' is on the body by default and counts toward skin-out weight but not pack weight or pack volume. TEN_ESSENTIALS uses the modern ten (navigation, headlamp, sun, first_aid, knife = knife plus repair kit, fire, shelter, extra_food, extra_water, extra_clothes); the planner's checklist lights up a slot when any carried item fills it. TIERS: top-level fields are the standard version; each tier entry overrides name, weight, volume, price and any stats it lists, and may add or remove tags. Items without tiers come in one version. TAGS are what the event engine reads (simulation.md 6.6): the packing code turns item tags and stats into derived trip tags, for example rain_top + rain_bottom, insulation:N = sum of stats.insulation, sleep:T from stats.temp_rating_f, padR from stats.r_value, shelter:tent/tarp/bivy/hammock/none from shelter_* tags, water_treat:*, water_capL from stats.liters, nav:* from nav_* tags, canister:L from stats.capacity_l. Every tag is defined in tag_glossary; key stats in stat_glossary. TRAPS: items tagged 'trap' are real mistakes people make (cotton, canned food lives in the food catalog, hang kits, drones). The store shows their true weight and the notes are honest, so a trap is a choice, never a trick. RULES baked into notes reflect the 2026 region data in design/data/regions: approved hard-sided bear canisters are required for every wilderness overnight, soft bear sacks are not on the approved list, hanging food is not acceptable, campfires are prohibited above 3,500 ft and were under a park-wide Stage 2 ban from August 2026, drones and plant collecting are prohibited, and no state fishing license is needed inside the park. NAMES: all product names are generic or fictional; '-class' size references (BV500-class etc.) appear only in notes as the sizes backpackers know, never as products for sale. Weights, volumes and prices are typical values sanity-checked against 2025-2026 retail listings and reviews, rounded for play. BASIC OR NICE (added 2026-10-09; GAME_DESIGN 5.8, Lead call 29): every item, pack and tier carries basic. An item-tier is basic, and free, when it is the plain, serviceable version of an essential: it meets a row of the ranger's checklist or the worn outfit (content/rules/kits.json), is a pack, or is the basic stove's fuel, and it is the plainest version of that thing on an M1a shelf (the cheap tier where one is sold; the general store's where both stores sell it). Every trap the general store sells is basic too, so the flat lay still teaches (5.8, decision 42). Everything else is nice, at its price_usd: the standard and premium tiers above a cheap one, light and technical gear, joy and fun items, the instruments. The flags are set by hand, item by item; tools/ingest/catalogs.mjs checks the rule's hard edges (IG15) and fails a catalog with no free basic for a checklist row, a pack or the basic stove's fuel (IG16). NEW ITEMS (2026-10-09): tarp_canvas, flannel_cotton, wool_pants_surplus and blanket_wool, the general store's from GAME_DESIGN 5.7, each estimate: true with its evidence by field; 223 items now. The socks carry stats.covers feet, and bombproof replaces unbreakable.

packs.name: Town Book Bag 20
packs.real_world_notes: A school or commuter bag: canvas or thin nylon, no hip belt, no frame, one bottle pocket. Fine for a 2-mile nature walk; on a 10-mile day with 3 L of water the shoulder straps cut in and the canvas soaks through in drizzle.
packs.flavor: The little bag has carried lunches and library books for years, and it looks surprised to be going up a mountain.

packs.name: Ridge Runner Daypack 28
packs.real_world_notes: A real hiking daypack: light framesheet, mesh back, webbing hip belt, room for the ten essentials, rain shell, puffy, 3 L of water and lunch. It cannot hold a sleeping bag, shelter and bear canister together, which is the point of the Mount Olympus warning.
packs.flavor: It holds everything a long day needs and not one thing more, like a well-packed lunch box.

packs.name: Featherline Fastpack 35
packs.real_world_notes: Enough for one or two summer nights only with an ultralight kit (quilt, trekking-pole tent, small canister). A BV500-class canister eats a third of it. Overloading past about 22 lb makes the hip belt fold and the shoulders ache.
packs.flavor: A quick, light pack for quick, light people who have already decided what they can live without.

packs.name: Lake Basin Weekender 50
packs.real_world_notes: The sweet spot for 2 to 4 nights in summer with a reasonably modern kit, including a full-size bear canister mounted vertically. Tight with a synthetic bag or a bulky tent.
packs.flavor: It is the kind of pack that has seen a hundred lakes and still has room for one more apple.

packs.name: Thru-Line Ultralight 55
packs.real_world_notes: Laminated waterproof-ish fabric and a minimal frame. Wonderful under 30 lb, punishing above it: the frame cannot transfer a heavy canister-plus-water load to the hips. Seams still leak in the Hoh, so use a liner anyway.
packs.flavor: It weighs almost nothing and asks only that you bring almost nothing.

packs.name: Hurricane Ridge Trekker 65
packs.real_world_notes: The classic 4 to 7 night pack with a stout frame and an adjustable torso. It carries a canister, a winter-ish bag and climbing hardware without complaint, and tempts you to fill every liter.
packs.flavor: A big, patient pack with a strong back, and it will carry whatever you ask, even the things you should have left at home.

packs.name: Blue Glacier Expedition 80
packs.real_world_notes: Built for glacier approaches, winter trips and long traverses: rope, crampons, a 0 °F bag and a week of food. Overkill for a summer weekend, where its own 5.5 lb becomes dead weight and the extra space invites overpacking.
packs.flavor: It is as tall as a fox standing on another fox, and it was made for the long road to the snow.

packs.name: Grandpa's External Frame 70
packs.real_world_notes: A garage-sale aluminum frame with a canvas bag. It carries heavy loads surprisingly well on smooth trail and stays cool on the back, but the high frame snags on blowdown and brush, sways on ladders and log crossings, and the bag is not waterproof.
packs.flavor: Its aluminum frame clinks like a wind chime, and it remembers trails that were built before you were born.

items.name: Two-Person Dome Tent

tiers.name: Bargain Bin Dome Tent
tiers.note: Fiberglass poles snap in cold wind; the short fly lets rain splash in.

tiers.name: Featherdome UL2
tiers.note: Semi-freestanding; thin floor wants a footprint on coast gravel.

items.real_world_notes: A double-wall 3-season dome. Pitches on rock, gravel bars and wooden tent pads where stakes won't go. Poles can ride in a side pocket to save inside volume. Split it with a partner: one carries the body, one the fly and poles.
items.flavor: A small round house of green nylon, just big enough for two sleepers and one pair of muddy boots.

items.name: Solo Trekking-Pole Tent

tiers.name: Cloudspun Solo (composite fabric)
tiers.note: Very light and does not sag when wet; costly.

items.real_world_notes: Pitched with your trekking poles instead of tent poles, so it is useless without them. Needs good stake ground; tricky on rock slabs, wooden platforms and loose beach sand without sand anchors.
items.flavor: It stands up tall on your two walking sticks, like a small kite that has decided to stay on the ground.

items.name: Three-Person Family Dome
items.real_world_notes: Roomy enough to play cards through a rainy layover. Heavy for one carrier; shared among three it is reasonable. Larger footprint is hard to fit on small designated tent pads.
items.flavor: There is room inside for three sleepers, a card game, and a long rainy afternoon.

items.name: Four-Season Mountain Tent
items.real_world_notes: Steep walls, extra poles, snow flaps. The right shelter for the Snow Dome high camp, winter Hurricane Ridge or a storm on an exposed ridge. Too hot and heavy for a summer valley.
items.flavor: Its walls are steep and its poles are many, and it does not mind when the wind sings all night.

items.name: Flat Tarp 8 x 10 with Cord and Stakes
items.real_world_notes: Light and versatile but needs skill: a good pitch takes practice, and sideways rain and wind on the High Divide or the coast find every gap. No bug protection. Can also be a midday rain kitchen for a group.
items.flavor: It is only a square of fabric, but in the right hands it becomes a roof, a porch, or a rainy-day kitchen.

items.name: Canvas Tarp 8 x 10

Bombproof: it never fails from wear.

items.name: Waterproof Bivy Sack
items.real_world_notes: A waterproof-breathable bag around your sleeping bag. Fine on a clear alpine night; miserable in a 12-hour Olympic rain because there is nowhere to change, cook or sit, and condensation dampens a down bag.
items.flavor: It is a sleeping bag for your sleeping bag, snug as a seed in its shell.

items.name: Emergency Reflective Bivy
items.real_world_notes: A reflective, waterproof sack for an unplanned night out. It turns a dangerous bivouac into a long, crinkly, damp one. Counts as the shelter essential on day hikes.
items.flavor: It crinkles like candy paper and holds your own warmth close, just in case the day runs longer than planned.

items.name: Foil Space Blanket
items.real_world_notes: Better than nothing and almost weightless, but it tears easily and blows away in wind. A day hiker's last line of defense.
items.flavor: A silver sheet as thin as a moth's wing, folded small and hoping never to be opened.

items.name: Plastic Tube Tent
items.real_world_notes: A cheap polyethylene tube strung on a cord between two trees. Open ends let rain blow through; condensation drips on you all night. Nostalgic, heavy for what it does.
items.flavor: It looks like a long plastic bread bag, and on a rainy night it feels like one, too.

items.name: Camping Hammock with Bug Net and Rain Fly
items.real_world_notes: Wonderful in the rain-forest valleys and on lumpy ground, impossible above treeline (High Divide meadows, Hoh Lake edges, beach sand). Cold from below without an underquilt or pad.
items.flavor: Strung between two old trees, it rocks you to sleep the way the wind rocks a nest.

items.name: Tent Footprint
items.real_world_notes: Protects a thin tent floor from coast gravel, sharp rock and mud. Optional on soft forest duff.
items.flavor: A thin sheet that keeps the tent floor safe from pebbles that would rather be poking.

items.name: Sand and Snow Stakes (set of 6)
items.real_world_notes: Wide stakes that hold in beach sand and soft snow, where thin wire stakes pull out. Useful on the wilderness coast and early-season high camps.
items.flavor: Broad little paddles that grip the sand and the snow when skinny stakes give up.

items.name: Down Sleeping Bag 30 °F

tiers.name: Down Sleeping Bag 30 °F (900 fill, water-resistant down)

items.real_world_notes: The standard Olympic summer bag. Most nights at 4,000 to 5,000 ft in July to August fall into the 35 to 50 °F range. Down loses most of its loft when soaked, so a pack liner matters in the Hoh and on the coast.
items.flavor: A soft cloud of feathers that remembers the warmth you give it and gives it back all night.

items.name: Down Sleeping Bag 20 °F

tiers.name: Down Sleeping Bag 20 °F (900 fill, water-resistant down)

items.real_world_notes: The safe choice for shoulder seasons (June and September to October) and for high camps such as Glacier Meadows, Seven Lakes Basin and Royal Basin, where frost is possible any month.
items.flavor: A thicker cloud, for nights when the stars are sharp and the meadow grass turns white with frost.

items.name: Down Expedition Bag 0 °F
items.real_world_notes: Winter and early-season summit camps only. In August it is a sauna that fills half a 50 L pack.
items.flavor: So puffy and warm that it could keep a snowbank cozy.

items.name: Synthetic Sleeping Bag 30 °F
items.real_world_notes: Cheaper and forgiving when damp, which counts for something in the rain forest and on the coast. But it is half again as heavy and nearly twice as bulky as down, which squeezes the bear canister out of a 50 L pack.
items.flavor: A plain, sturdy bag that stays warm even when the clouds come inside the tent.

items.name: Synthetic Sleeping Bag 20 °F
items.real_world_notes: Warm and wet-tolerant, but 4 lb and enormous. It nearly fills a 50 L pack together with a canister and tent. A classic 'it won't close' item.
items.flavor: It is warm as a bear's winter den, and nearly as big.

items.name: Summer Synthetic Bag 45 °F
items.real_world_notes: Fine for low coastal camps in August. Cold at any subalpine camp; needs a puffy worn to bed or a liner.
items.flavor: A thin summer bag, good for warm beaches and nights that smell of salt and driftwood.

items.name: Flannel-Lined Rectangular Bag
items.real_world_notes: A car-camping bag. The cotton flannel lining soaks up damp and never dries; at 6 lb and the size of a beach ball it rides outside the pack, where the rain finds it. A trap.
items.flavor: It has ducks printed on the lining and smells like the cabin, but it was never meant to climb mountains.

items.name: Down Backpacking Quilt 30 °F
items.real_world_notes: No hood and an open back; relies on the sleeping pad below and a warm hat. Drafty for restless sleepers or windy, cold nights.
items.flavor: Like a feather blanket from home that learned to tuck itself in.

items.name: Down Backpacking Quilt 20 °F
items.real_world_notes: A popular 3-season ultralight choice. Pair with a pad of R 3 or more and a beanie.
items.flavor: Warm and light as a snowfall that never melts.

items.name: Silk Sleeping Bag Liner
items.real_world_notes: Adds a few degrees and keeps the bag cleaner. Small gain for small weight.
items.flavor: Smooth as a ribbon, it slips inside your bag and adds a little warmth.

items.name: Fleece Sleeping Bag Liner
items.real_world_notes: A cheap way to stretch a 40 °F bag toward 30 °F. Bulky for what it does.
items.flavor: A fuzzy sleeve of fleece that makes a summer bag brave enough for autumn.

items.name: Compression Stuff Sack
items.real_world_notes: Squeezes a sleeping bag or puffy to about 70% of its stuffed volume. The trick that makes a canister and a bag share a small pack.
items.flavor: Pull the straps and the puffy bag sighs and shrinks, as if holding its breath.

items.name: Closed-Cell Foam Pad (accordion)
items.real_world_notes: Can't puncture, doubles as a sit pad, works as a pack frame sheet. Too bulky to fit inside, so it rides on the outside in rain and brush. Alone it is cold below about 40 °F; stacked under an inflatable it adds R 2.
items.flavor: A folding mat of bumpy foam that never pops and never complains.

items.name: Torso-Length Foam Pad
items.real_world_notes: An ultralight trick: shoulders to hips only, with the pack under your legs. Cold feet on cold nights.
items.flavor: Half a mat for half a sleeper, and the other half is up to you.

items.name: Insulated Inflatable Pad (R 4)
items.real_world_notes: Warm, comfortable, packs small. Can puncture, especially if strapped outside on brushy trail or used on sharp beach gravel; a patch kit fixes most leaks. Inflate with a pump sack in cold weather to keep breath moisture out.
items.flavor: Blow it up with twenty breaths and it becomes a soft, warm raft for the night.

items.name: Self-Inflating Foam Pad (R 3.5)
items.real_world_notes: Durable and comfortable but heavy and bulky; often ends up strapped under the pack.
items.flavor: It unrolls with a slow, sleepy sigh as it fills itself with air.

items.name: Inflatable Pillow
items.real_world_notes: Better sleep for 2.6 oz. A stuff sack full of clothes works too.
items.flavor: A little cloud for your head, small enough to fit in your fist.

items.name: Cotton T-Shirt
items.real_world_notes: 'Cotton kills': cotton holds water, loses all insulation when wet and stays wet. On a 55 °F rainy day in the Hoh it chills you even while you hike. Fine for the car ride home.
items.flavor: Soft and comfy in town, but on a misty trail it drinks up the rain and holds onto the cold.

items.name: Blue Jeans
items.real_world_notes: Heavy when dry, twice as heavy when wet, restrict knee movement on high steps, chafe, and never dry in Olympic humidity. The classic trap item.
items.flavor: Stiff and sturdy as a barn door, and just as heavy once the rain soaks in.

items.name: Cotton Hoodie Sweatshirt
items.real_world_notes: Cozy at camp only if it stays perfectly dry. Damp hoodies are cold hoodies. Takes the volume of a puffy for a third of the warmth.
items.flavor: A cuddly old sweatshirt that turns heavy and gray as soon as the fog finds it.

items.name: Synthetic Hiking Tee
items.real_world_notes: Wicks and dries fast; smells strongly after day two.
items.flavor: Light as a leaf and quick to dry, though by the third day it smells like a busy trail.

items.name: Merino Wool Tee
items.real_world_notes: Comfortable over a range of temperatures, resists odor for days, still warm-ish when damp. Pricier and less durable than synthetic.
items.flavor: A soft wool shirt that keeps you warm when it's cool and cool when it's warm, like a sheep's own coat.

items.name: Synthetic Long-Sleeve Base Layer
items.real_world_notes: A light warm layer for hiking in cool mist or sleeping. Kept dry in a stuff sack, it doubles as the camp shirt.
items.flavor: A thin, stretchy layer that fits close and keeps the chill from sneaking in.

items.name: Merino Long-Sleeve Base Layer
items.real_world_notes: The favorite sleeping and camp layer for multi-day trips. Kept dry, it is the reward at the end of a wet day.
items.flavor: Pulling on this dry wool shirt at camp feels like coming home.

items.name: Synthetic Long Underwear Bottoms
items.real_world_notes: Warm legs at camp and in the sleeping bag; adds several degrees to a bag's comfort.
items.flavor: A pair of thin, warm leggings that make a cold sleeping bag feel friendlier.

items.name: Merino Long Underwear Bottoms
items.real_world_notes: As above, in wool: warmer when damp, less smelly.
items.flavor: Wool leggings for the frosty hours between supper and sunrise.

items.name: Nylon Hiking Pants
items.real_world_notes: Dry quickly, shed light drizzle, protect legs from devil's club, nettles, salal and mosquitoes on overgrown trails.
items.flavor: Tough, light trousers that brush past nettles and thorns without a scratch.

items.name: Hiking Shorts
items.real_world_notes: Cool on hot climbs like the Hoh Lake switchbacks or Appleton Pass. Bare legs get wet and scratched in brushy, dewy meadows.
items.flavor: Breezy shorts for sunny switchbacks and knees that like the fresh air.

items.name: Convertible Zip-Off Pants
items.real_world_notes: Pants in the morning dew, shorts on the afternoon climb. The zippers chafe some hikers.
items.flavor: Trousers in the morning and shorts by noon, with a zip in between.

items.name: Surplus Wool Pants

items.real_world_notes: New for the general store (GAME_DESIGN 5.7, added 2026-10-09): surplus wool trousers, heavy and warm when wet. Every number is an estimate: weight and price from 5.7's table, the volume from jeans_denim, the warmth from the catalog's wool items.

items.name: Synthetic Underwear (2 pairs)
items.real_world_notes: Two pairs: wear one, rinse and dry one. Cotton underwear chafes badly on long, wet days.
items.flavor: Two pairs that take turns: one on the trail and one drying on the tent line.

items.name: Cotton Tube Socks (3 pairs)
items.real_world_notes: Wet cotton socks bunch, rub and soften skin; the fastest way to blisters on a long descent.
items.flavor: Bright white socks that slump and squish as soon as your boots get damp.

items.name: Wool Hiking Socks (2 pairs)
items.real_world_notes: Two pairs minimum, plus a dedicated dry pair for sleeping. Wool stays warm when damp and resists blisters.
items.flavor: Thick wool socks that hug your feet like a pair of friendly sheep.

items.name: Thin Liner Socks (2 pairs)
items.real_world_notes: Worn under hiking socks to reduce friction. Some hikers swear by them, others never use them.
items.flavor: Two thin socks that slide against each other, so your skin doesn't have to.

items.name: Waterproof Membrane Socks
items.real_world_notes: Keep feet warm and dry-ish in trail runners on wet trails and snow. Sweaty in warm weather; overtopped by deep fords.
items.flavor: Socks with a secret raincoat inside them.

items.name: Down Camp Booties
items.real_world_notes: Pure camp and sleeping luxury for cold-footed hikers. Useless wet.
items.flavor: Puffy slippers that make your toes forget they ever walked ten miles.

items.name: Fleece Jacket (100 weight)
items.real_world_notes: Warm when damp, breathable, cheap, durable. Lets wind through and does not compress, so it is bulkier than its warmth suggests.
items.flavor: A fuzzy jacket, warm as a sheepdog's coat, that doesn't mind a little mist.

items.name: Grid Fleece Hoody
items.real_world_notes: An active layer for cold mornings and windy passes: breathes while you climb.
items.flavor: A light, checkered fleece that keeps you warm on the move without letting you overheat.

items.name: Down Puffy Jacket
items.real_world_notes: The camp jacket. The most warmth per ounce, crucial on evenings at Glacier Meadows or watching the sunset from Bogachiel Peak. Keep it dry: wear it under the rain shell only at camp, never while hiking in rain.
items.flavor: A jacket made of warm air and feathers, perfect for sitting still and watching the sky turn gold.

items.name: Synthetic Puffy Jacket
items.real_world_notes: A bit heavier and bulkier than down, but it keeps working in the coast's sea fog and the rain forest's drizzle.
items.flavor: A puffy coat that keeps its promise even when the fog rolls in from the sea.

items.name: Down Vest
items.real_world_notes: Core warmth with free arms. A summer layer that is not enough on its own for a cold night.
items.flavor: A puffy vest that keeps your middle warm and leaves your arms free to point at things.

items.name: Down Camp Pants
items.real_world_notes: Shoulder-season and summit-camp luxury. Turn a 30 °F bag into a 20 °F system.
items.flavor: Puffy trousers that make a cold evening feel like sitting by a stove.

items.name: Wind Shell Jacket
items.real_world_notes: Blocks wind on the High Divide and at passes, breathes on the climb, and weighs almost nothing. Not rain gear.
items.flavor: A whisper-thin jacket that tells the wind politely to go around.

items.name: Old Wool Sweater
items.real_world_notes: A thrift-store Fair Isle sweater. Warm even when damp, as old-timers knew, but heavy and bulky next to modern layers.
items.flavor: Grandmother knitted it before anyone said 'ultralight', and it is still warm as toast.

items.name: Wool Beanie
items.real_world_notes: Cheap warmth for 2 oz. Sleep in it.
items.flavor: A wool cap with a little pompom, the warmest two ounces you will ever carry.

items.name: Balaclava
items.real_world_notes: Face and neck protection for summit wind and winter.
items.flavor: A hood that keeps your cheeks warm when the summit wind bites.

items.name: Liner Gloves
items.real_world_notes: Light gloves for cold mornings, trekking poles and fiddling with the stove.
items.flavor: Thin gloves for chilly fingers that still want to tie knots.

items.name: Insulated Waterproof Gloves
items.real_world_notes: Needed for snow travel, ice axe work and the Blue Glacier. Wet hands go numb fast on snow.
items.flavor: Thick gloves that keep your fingers warm while you hold the cold handle of an ice axe.

items.name: Neck Gaiter Tube
items.real_world_notes: Sun shield, warm hat, headband or dust mask in one tube.
items.flavor: A stretchy tube that can be a hat, a scarf, or a sun shade, whatever the day needs.

items.name: Cotton Bandana
items.real_world_notes: The one cotton item backpackers love: a sweat rag, sun shade, pot grabber, pre-filter for silty glacial water and emergency sling. Being wet is the point.
items.flavor: A square of red cloth with a hundred jobs and no complaints.

items.name: Rain Jacket

tiers.name: Budget Rain Jacket (2.5-layer)
tiers.note: Wets out within an hour of steady rain; clammy on climbs.

items.real_world_notes: Non-negotiable on the Olympic Peninsula, where the west-side valleys get 140 to 170 inches of rain a year and summer showers can happen anywhere. Even the best jacket wets out after hours of steady rain; you hike damp but warm.
items.flavor: A crinkly jacket with a hood, the most important thing in the pack on a mountain where the clouds live.

items.name: Rain Pants
items.real_world_notes: Often left behind to save space, and then missed: wet brush soaks your legs even after the rain stops (Bogachiel, upper Hoh, coastal overland trails). Also a warm layer at a windy camp.
items.flavor: Swishy trousers that keep your knees dry when the meadow grass is full of last night's rain.

items.name: Hooded Rain Poncho
items.real_world_notes: Covers you and your pack and breathes well, but flaps like a sail in wind on ridges and the coast and snags on brush. Leaves the lower legs wet.
items.flavor: A big green cape that keeps the rain off both you and your pack, as long as the wind stays calm.

items.name: Silnylon Poncho-Tarp
items.real_world_notes: Rain gear by day and a tiny lean-to by night. A real shelter only for skilled minimalists in mild weather; in a storm you have neither a dry shelter nor dry clothes.
items.flavor: By day it is a raincoat, and by night it becomes a tiny roof, if you know the trick.

items.name: Hiking Umbrella
items.real_world_notes: Wonderful in the windless rain-forest valleys (Hoh, Quinault, Bogachiel): no sweaty hood, and you can read the map. Useless on the windy High Divide or the coast, and awkward on overgrown trail.
items.flavor: Under its dome the rain sounds like popcorn, and the forest stays quiet and green around you.

items.name: Pack Rain Cover
items.real_world_notes: Sheds most rain but water still runs down your back into the pack, and it blows off in wind. Better with a liner.
items.flavor: A shower cap for your backpack.

items.name: Trash-Compactor Bag Pack Liner
items.real_world_notes: The cheapest serious waterproofing: line the pack, put the sleeping bag and dry clothes inside, twist the top. Survives a fall in a ford. Replace when punctured.
items.flavor: A plain plastic bag, and the reason your sleeping bag is still dry after a day of rain.

items.name: Roll-Top Pack Liner (50 L)
items.real_world_notes: A tougher, reusable version of the compactor bag.
items.flavor: A tough, rolled-top bag that keeps the inside of your pack as dry as a cupboard.

items.name: Small Dry Bag (5 L)
items.real_world_notes: For dry camp clothes, electronics and the map. Dry clothes at camp are the single biggest comfort in the Olympics.
items.flavor: A little waterproof sack for the things that must stay dry no matter what.

items.name: Large Dry Bag (20 L)
items.real_world_notes: Makes a sleeping bag strapped outside the pack survive the rain.
items.flavor: A big waterproof sack, roomy enough to keep a whole sleeping bag dry.

items.name: Gallon Zip Bags (10)
items.real_world_notes: Map case, phone sleeve, trash bag, food repackaging. Pack out every wrapper.
items.flavor: Ten clear bags for maps, snacks, socks and the wrappers you will carry home.

items.name: Trail Running Shoes
items.real_world_notes: Light, comfortable, and dry fast after fords and rain. They will get wet on Olympic trails, so plan for wet feet and good socks. Less support with heavy loads and less protection on scree and snow.
items.flavor: Light shoes that splash through puddles and dry again by lunchtime.

items.name: Waterproof Mid Hiking Boots
items.real_world_notes: Dry in puddles and light rain, supportive under a heavy pack. Once water comes over the top (fords, all-day rain) they stay wet for days. Break them in before the trip: new boots are a blister machine.
items.flavor: Sturdy boots that keep the puddles out, until the day the river comes over the top.

items.name: Full-Grain Leather Backpacking Boots
items.real_world_notes: Bombproof support for heavy loads, scree and kicking steps in snow. Heavy: a pound on the feet costs about as much energy as several pounds on the back.
items.flavor: Heavy leather boots that clomp like a pony and last as long as one.

items.name: Crampon-Compatible Mountaineering Boots
items.real_world_notes: Stiff soles for kicking steps and wearing strap or hybrid crampons on the Blue Glacier and Snow Dome. Miserable for the 17 forest miles up the Hoh; most climbers carry them and hike in lighter shoes. Commonly rented.
items.flavor: Stiff as a pair of wooden clogs, these boots were made to bite into snow and ice.

items.name: Canvas Sneakers
items.real_world_notes: Cotton canvas uppers and smooth soles: slippery on wet roots, rocks and ladders, soggy for days. A trap.
items.flavor: Fine for the school yard, but their smooth soles slide on wet roots like butter on a pan.

items.name: Strap Sport Sandals
items.real_world_notes: Ford shoes and camp shoes in one: secure heel straps for the Queets ford, the Elwha or coast creeks, and dry boots afterward. Toes are exposed to rocks.
items.flavor: Strappy sandals that grip the river stones while your boots ride safe and dry on your pack.

items.name: Foam Camp Clogs
items.real_world_notes: Let tired, wrinkled feet dry out at camp. Fine for shallow creek crossings, but they float away in real current.
items.flavor: Squishy clogs for the evening, when your feet have done their work and want to rest.

items.name: Flip-Flops
items.real_world_notes: Light camp shoes, but the worst ford shoes: they pull off in current and leave you barefoot on slick rocks.
items.flavor: Flip, flop, flip, flop, until the river takes one away to the sea.

items.name: Low Trail Gaiters
items.real_world_notes: Keep sand, pebbles and fir needles out of trail runners. Handy on coast beaches.
items.flavor: Little cuffs that keep pebbles from sneaking into your shoes.

items.name: Tall Waterproof Gaiters
items.real_world_notes: For snowfields, postholing, muddy trail and wet brush. Standard kit for Glacier Meadows and early-season passes.
items.flavor: Tall leggings that keep the snow and mud on the outside, where they belong.

items.name: Canister Stove (upright)
items.real_world_notes: Light, simple, allowed during most fire bans because it has a shut-off valve. Weak in cold and wind; a windscreen (never wrapped tightly around the canister) helps. Needs a separately sold fuel canister and a lighter.
items.flavor: A tiny folding stove that blooms with a blue flower of flame.

items.name: Integrated Canister Stove System
items.real_world_notes: Stove and heat-exchanger pot in one: fast, fuel-efficient, wind-resistant, but poor for real cooking or simmering. A 110 g canister nests inside.
items.flavor: Stove and pot fit together like an acorn in its cap, and the water boils before you can count your mosquito bites.

items.name: Alcohol Can Stove
items.real_world_notes: Ultralight and silent, but slow, nearly invisible flame, and no shut-off valve. Typically prohibited under Stage 2 fire restrictions, and Olympic had a park-wide Stage 2 ban in late summer 2026.
items.flavor: A little tin cup that burns with a pale flame you can barely see, so watch your sleeves.

items.name: White-Gas Liquid-Fuel Stove
items.real_world_notes: Works in deep cold and for melting snow on a glacier camp. Heavier, needs priming and pumping, and can flare if mishandled.
items.flavor: It roars like a little jet engine, and it is happiest on the coldest morning of the trip.

items.name: Fuel Canister 110 g
items.real_world_notes: Isobutane-propane mix. About 14 half-liter boils in mild, calm weather, fewer in cold and wind. Enough for 2 to 3 nights of boil-only cooking for one person. Cannot be mailed or flown; buy it in town.
items.flavor: A small round can full of tomorrow morning's coffee.

items.name: Fuel Canister 230 g
items.real_world_notes: About 30 half-liter boils. Right for a week solo or 3 to 4 nights for two.
items.flavor: A bigger can of blue flame, for longer trips and more hot chocolate.

items.name: Fuel Canister 450 g
items.real_world_notes: For groups, winter trips and snow melting.
items.flavor: A heavy can, big enough for a whole group's suppers or a pot full of melted snow.

items.name: Denatured Alcohol (8 fl oz bottle)
items.real_world_notes: Fuel for the alcohol stove. Store it far from food; leaks taint everything.
items.flavor: A small bottle of clear fuel, labeled carefully so no one mistakes it for water.

items.name: White Gas (20 fl oz fuel bottle, full)
items.real_world_notes: Fuel for the liquid-fuel stove, with a refillable aluminum bottle.
items.flavor: A red metal bottle sloshing with fuel for cold mornings on the glacier.

items.name: Titanium Pot 750 mL
items.real_world_notes: A one-person boil pot and mug in one. A small canister and stove nest inside, so it takes almost no extra volume.
items.flavor: A shiny little pot that holds the stove, the fuel, and later, the soup.

items.name: Aluminum Cook Pot 1.3 L with Lid
items.real_world_notes: Right for two people or for real cooking (pasta sides, rice). Spreads heat well for simmering.
items.flavor: A dented, friendly pot that has cooked a hundred suppers for two.

items.name: Cast-Iron Skillet
items.real_world_notes: Five pounds of cast iron for camp pancakes. It works, it tastes wonderful, and it hurts every step of the way. A trap with a happy ending.
items.flavor: Heavy as a sleeping cat and twice as stubborn, it makes the best pancakes on the whole mountain.

items.name: Long-Handled Titanium Spoon
items.real_world_notes: A long handle reaches the bottom of a meal pouch without messy fingers.
items.flavor: A long spoon for reaching the very last bite at the bottom of the bag.

items.name: Insulated Camp Mug
items.real_world_notes: A hot drink that stays hot. Often clipped to the outside of the pack, where it clanks and sometimes vanishes in the brush.
items.flavor: A cup to wrap both hands around while the morning mist lifts off the lake.

items.name: Mini Lighter
items.real_world_notes: Carry two: one in the cook kit, one in the first aid kit. Butane lighters struggle when cold; keep one in a pocket.
items.flavor: A small lighter that clicks and gives a little flame, the size of your thumb.

items.name: Storm-Proof Matches with Strikers
items.real_world_notes: Burn even after being dunked; the ten-essentials fire backup.
items.flavor: Matches that keep burning even when the wind blows and the rain falls.

items.name: Firestarter Cubes
items.real_world_notes: For an emergency fire, which is allowed in a true emergency even during bans. Campfires are otherwise prohibited above 3,500 ft in Olympic and under seasonal bans.
items.flavor: Little waxy blocks that help a struggling fire catch, for emergencies only.

items.name: Folding Stove Windscreen
items.real_world_notes: Saves fuel on windy ridges. With canister stoves, never fully enclose the canister (overheating).
items.flavor: A little fence that keeps the wind from stealing your flame.

items.name: Cold-Soak Jar (screw-top)
items.real_world_notes: A washed-out peanut butter jar for no-stove meals: add couscous, ramen, oats or beans and water, wait 30 to 90 minutes. Saves the stove's weight but no hot meals.
items.flavor: An old peanut butter jar that turns noodles soft with nothing but water and patience.

items.name: Collapsible Pour-Over Coffee Dripper
items.real_world_notes: Real coffee at the lake. Grounds must be packed out (they don't belong in the creek or soil).
items.flavor: A folding coffee cone, so the morning can smell like home, even at the edge of a mountain lake.

items.name: Biodegradable Soap and Scrubber
items.real_world_notes: A few drops for pots and hands, used 200 ft from lakes and streams. Goes in the canister at night (scented).
items.flavor: A tiny bottle of soap that smells faintly of peppermint, for washing up far from the lake.

items.name: Squeeze Water Filter
items.real_world_notes: Fast and light. Removes bacteria and protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), not viruses (low risk in the backcountry here). If it freezes it can crack invisibly: sleep with it on frosty nights. Glacial silt from the Hoh and Elwha clogs it; settle water or pre-filter through a bandana.
items.flavor: A soft pouch and a small filter that turn creek water into drinking water with a gentle squeeze.

items.name: Pump Water Filter
items.real_world_notes: Draws from shallow seeps and small pools on the High Divide crest where you can't dip a bottle. Heavier; the cartridge can be scrubbed when silt clogs it.
items.flavor: Pump, pump, pump, and the clear water trickles into your bottle, one splash at a time.

items.name: Gravity Filter 4 L
items.real_world_notes: Hang it on a branch and do camp chores while it filters. Great for groups and layover days.
items.flavor: Hang the bag on a branch and let gravity do the work while you set up camp.

items.name: UV Light Purifier Pen
items.real_world_notes: Kills viruses too, but fails in silty or tannic water (glacial Hoh and Elwha, tea-colored coast creeks) and needs a charged battery. The bulb is glass.
items.flavor: A little wand that glows blue in the water, like a firefly that keeps you healthy.

items.name: Chlorine Dioxide Tablets (30)
items.real_world_notes: Light, foolproof backup if a filter breaks or freezes. Thirty minutes for most pathogens, four hours for Cryptosporidium. Slight chlorine taste.
items.flavor: Tiny tablets that fizz in your bottle and ask you to wait half an hour.

items.name: Two-Part Chlorine Dioxide Drops
items.real_world_notes: Cheap treatment for a group. Mixing two drops and waiting five minutes before adding takes some fiddling with cold fingers.
items.flavor: Two little bottles: mix them, wait, and then the water is ready.

items.name: 1 L Disposable Water Bottle
items.real_world_notes: The hiker standard: light, fits side pockets and threads onto squeeze filters. Weighs 2.2 lb when full.
items.flavor: A plain, light bottle that rides in your side pocket and fills at every creek.

items.name: 1 L Hard Plastic Bottle
items.real_world_notes: Nearly indestructible. On a cold night, fill it with hot water, close it tightly and tuck it in the sleeping bag.
items.flavor: A tough bottle that can be filled with hot water and hugged on a frosty night.

items.name: Insulated Steel Bottle 0.75 L
items.real_world_notes: Heavy for a water bottle, but tea stays hot from breakfast to the summit.
items.flavor: It keeps your tea hot all the way to the top of the pass.

items.name: 2 L Hydration Bladder
items.real_world_notes: Hands-free sipping keeps you drinking on climbs, but you can't see how much is left, and it is hard to refill in a full pack.
items.flavor: A soft water bag with a long straw, so you can sip without stopping.

items.name: Collapsible 3 L Water Bag
items.real_world_notes: Carry water up to a dry camp or a dry crest (the High Divide in late summer) and saves trips to the lake.
items.flavor: It folds as flat as a pancake and fills up as round as a pumpkin.

items.name: Olympic Mountains Waterproof Topo Map
items.real_world_notes: A waterproof topographic trail map of the whole park. With a compass and the skill to use it, it finds the way when fog hides the High Divide cairns or snow buries the trail. Paper never runs out of battery.
items.flavor: A folded map with all the rivers drawn in blue and all the mountains drawn in wiggly brown rings.

items.name: Park Brochure Map
items.real_world_notes: The free visitor map from the entrance station is for driving, not for finding a trail junction in fog. Better than nothing; not a real navigation map.
items.flavor: A cheerful little map that shows the roads, the visitor centers, and not much else.

items.name: Wilderness Coast Strip Map
items.real_world_notes: Shows which headlands can be rounded only at low tide, which are impassable, and where the overland trails and rope ladders are, with the tide height each point needs. Essential with a tide table.
items.flavor: A long, skinny map of the coast, with little red marks where the sea comes all the way up to the cliffs.

items.name: Tide Table Booklet
items.real_world_notes: Coast hikers must know when the tide is low enough to round each headland. A phone app works only while the battery lasts. Needs a time source (watch or phone).
items.flavor: A thin booklet that knows exactly when the sea will breathe in and when it will breathe out.

items.name: Baseplate Compass with Declination
items.real_world_notes: With a topo map, the most reliable way to hold a bearing across a whited-out snowfield or meadow. Magnetic declination on the Peninsula is about 15° east.
items.flavor: A clear compass with a red needle that always remembers which way is north.

items.name: Keychain Button Compass
items.real_world_notes: Tells you roughly which way is north, not a bearing. A toy, not a tool.
items.flavor: A tiny compass on a keyring that wobbles and guesses.

items.name: Handheld GPS
items.real_world_notes: Shows exactly where you are, even on a buried trail. Batteries die in cold; carry spares.
items.flavor: A sturdy little screen with a dot that shows exactly where you are standing.

items.name: Smartphone
items.real_world_notes: Already owned (price 0). In airplane mode with downloaded offline maps it is a decent GPS, clock, camera and dim flashlight. Cell service is absent in almost all of the park's backcountry. Cold, rain and a dropped phone end its usefulness.
items.flavor: Your telephone, which up here becomes a camera, a clock, and a map, but rarely a telephone.

items.name: Offline Topo Map App (annual)
items.real_world_notes: Turns the phone into a GPS with topo maps, if the maps were downloaded at home before the trip. Weightless but battery-limited.
items.flavor: Maps that live inside your telephone and need no paper at all, only a little battery.

items.name: Power Bank 10,000 mAh
items.real_world_notes: About 2 to 3 phone charges. Enough for 3 to 5 days of careful phone use.
items.flavor: A small brick that stores electricity, like a snack for your telephone.

items.name: Power Bank 20,000 mAh
items.real_world_notes: For long trips or heavy camera and GPS use. Weighs as much as a day of food.
items.flavor: A bigger brick with a week's worth of electricity inside.

items.name: Satellite Messenger with SOS
items.real_world_notes: Two-way texts and an SOS button that work almost anywhere under open sky; deep forest and canyon walls slow or block messages. A rescue still takes hours to days in the Olympics. Requires a subscription.
items.flavor: A small orange box that can whisper to the satellites, so someone always knows where you are.

items.name: Altimeter Watch
items.real_world_notes: Time for the tides and the turnaround, altitude for finding where you are on a long climb. A falling barometer warns of an incoming front.
items.flavor: A wristwatch that knows how high you are and whether the weather is changing its mind.

items.name: Plain Digital Watch
items.real_world_notes: A reliable clock for tide windows and alpine starts that never runs out of battery on a trip.
items.flavor: A simple watch that beeps at dawn and keeps time with the tides.

items.name: Trail Guidebook to the Olympics
items.real_world_notes: Trail descriptions, mileages and history. Most hikers photocopy the relevant pages instead of carrying the whole book.
items.flavor: A well-thumbed book that tells you what is around the next bend, and who named it.

items.name: Headlamp
items.real_world_notes: A headlamp is the difference between an awkward late arrival and a night lost on the trail. Every party member needs their own. Tree cover in the river valleys makes it dark well before official sunset.
items.flavor: A small light worn on your forehead, so your hands are free and the dark is a little smaller.

items.name: Spare AAA Batteries (3)
items.real_world_notes: Spare batteries for the headlamp or GPS. Lithium cells work better in the cold.
items.flavor: Three little batteries, waiting quietly in case the night is long.

items.name: Big D-Cell Flashlight
items.real_world_notes: Heavy, needs a free hand, and the beam wobbles while you walk. A nostalgic trap; a headlamp does the job at an eighth of the weight.
items.flavor: A long silver flashlight from the kitchen drawer, heavy as a rolling pin.

items.name: Inflatable Solar Lantern
items.real_world_notes: A soft glow in the tent. Charges poorly under rain-forest canopy and in fog.
items.flavor: A glowing paper-lantern ball that makes the tent feel like a little house.

items.name: Basic First Aid Kit
items.real_world_notes: Handles cuts, scrapes and headaches. Not enough for a sprain or a bad fall far from the road.
items.flavor: A small red pouch with bandages, tape, and a little bottle of courage.

items.name: Comprehensive Backcountry First Aid Kit
items.real_world_notes: Manages a sprain, a deep cut or a wet, cold companion long enough to walk out or wait for help.
items.flavor: A thicker pouch with a little booklet inside, for the days when something goes truly wrong.

items.name: Blister Kit
items.real_world_notes: Treat hot spots the moment you feel them; a blister on day one can end a five-day trip. Wet feet in the Olympics make this especially important.
items.flavor: Tape and patches for feet that have walked too far in damp socks.

items.name: Trail Medicine Kit
items.real_world_notes: A few doses each of pain relief, allergy, stomach and electrolyte medicine. Bring any personal prescriptions.
items.flavor: A tiny case of pills and powders, each one a small comfort for a hard day.

items.name: Moldable Foam Splint
items.real_world_notes: Stabilizes an injured ankle or wrist for a slow walk out. Also improvised from a foam pad and trekking poles.
items.flavor: A soft metal strip that bends into whatever shape a hurt ankle needs.

items.name: Hand Sanitizer (2 oz)
items.real_world_notes: Most 'trail sickness' is passed hand to mouth, not through water. Clean hands after the cathole and before dinner. Scented; it goes in the canister.
items.flavor: A small bottle that keeps unseen germs from joining you for supper.

items.name: Toothbrush, Toothpaste and Lip Balm
items.real_world_notes: Toothpaste and lip balm are smellables that must go in the bear canister at night. Spit toothpaste 200 ft from water and camp.
items.flavor: A small toothbrush, a tiny tube of minty paste, and a stick of balm for windburned lips.

items.name: Basic Repair Kit
items.real_world_notes: Fixes a broken buckle, torn strap, blown seam or flapping sole well enough to finish the trip.
items.flavor: Pins, thread, tape and a spare buckle, for mending what the trail has torn.

items.name: Sleeping Pad Patch Kit
items.real_world_notes: Without it, a punctured air pad is a cold, sleepless night on the ground.
items.flavor: Six little patches that turn a sad, flat pad back into a bed.

items.name: Gear Repair Tape Patches
items.real_world_notes: Sticky patches for torn rain jackets, tents and down puffies leaking feathers.
items.flavor: Sticky patches that hold in the feathers when a puffy jacket gets a tear.

items.name: Tent Pole Repair Sleeve
items.real_world_notes: Splints a cracked tent pole so the tent stands through the night.
items.flavor: A short metal tube that hugs a broken tent pole until it is strong again.

items.name: Whole Roll of Duct Tape
items.real_world_notes: A whole roll fixes everything and weighs 10 oz. Wrapping 5 ft around a trekking pole or bottle does the same job for an ounce.
items.flavor: A big silver roll of tape, ready to fix everything twice, or ten times.

items.name: Seam Sealer Tube
items.real_world_notes: Fixes a leaking tent seam, but it has to cure for hours. Better done at home.
items.flavor: A small tube of glue that stops a leaky tent from dripping on your nose.

items.name: Sunscreen SPF 50 (3 oz)
items.real_world_notes: Snowfields and high meadows reflect strong sun, even on cool days. Sunscreen is scented, so it goes in the canister at night.
items.flavor: Creamy lotion that keeps your nose from turning as pink as a salmonberry.

items.name: Sunglasses
items.real_world_notes: Fine for trail and meadow. Too little for long snow travel.
items.flavor: Dark glasses for bright meadows and glittering lakes.

items.name: Glacier Glasses (category 4, side shields)
items.real_world_notes: Required for the Blue Glacier and the Snow Dome: hours on bright snow without them cause snow blindness, a painful sunburn of the eyes that appears that night.
items.flavor: Very dark glasses with little side shields, so the snow cannot dazzle you.

items.name: Wide-Brim Sun Hat
items.real_world_notes: Shades the face and neck on exposed climbs, sheds light rain off glasses.
items.flavor: A floppy hat with a wide brim, like a small umbrella for sunny days.

items.name: Ball Cap
items.real_world_notes: Shades the eyes, leaves ears and neck to burn.
items.flavor: A cap with a curved brim, good for keeping the sun out of your eyes.

items.name: UPF Sun Hoody
items.real_world_notes: Sun protection without reapplying sunscreen, and a light bug barrier. Popular for long exposed days.
items.flavor: A thin, airy shirt with a hood that keeps the sun off your neck and arms.

items.name: SPF Lip Balm
items.real_world_notes: Sun and wind crack lips quickly on snow. A smellable for the canister.
items.flavor: A tiny stick that keeps wind and sun from chapping your smile.

items.name: Bear Canister, Standard 11.5 L

tiers.name: Carbon-Fiber Bear Canister (10.6 L)
tiers.note: Lighter and costlier; slightly smaller inside.

items.real_world_notes: Required for every overnight in Olympic wilderness in 2026: food, trash and every scented item go inside at night, and hanging is not allowed. Holds about 5 person-days of food (the BV500-class size most backpackers know). volume_l is the outside size; capacity_l is what fits inside. Free loaners at the Port Angeles WIC when available.
items.flavor: A sturdy plastic barrel with a twist lid, the one thing a hungry bear cannot open.

items.name: Bear Canister, Small 7.2 L
items.real_world_notes: The BV450-class size. Fits a fastpack and holds about 3 person-days of food. Great for one or two nights solo; on longer trips the food simply won't fit.
items.flavor: A smaller barrel, just right for a short trip and a careful eater.

items.name: Bear Canister, Classic Opaque 10 L
items.real_world_notes: The heavy, black workhorse common in loaner fleets. The coin latches are fiddly with cold fingers; carry a coin or use a spoon handle.
items.flavor: A heavy black drum with two little locks that open with a coin and a bit of patience.

items.name: Loaner Bear Canister (free from the WIC)
items.real_world_notes: The Port Angeles Wilderness Information Center lends canisters free, first come, first served, with no reservations (the Quinault station was closed in 2026); it has a large supply but occasionally runs out over exceptionally busy weekends. Return it after the trip. In game the ranger desk always has one to lend, so a hiker with an empty shed and $0 is never stranded (GAME_DESIGN Lead call 33).
items.flavor: A well-traveled canister with scuffs from a hundred trips, borrowed from the rangers and returned with thanks.

items.name: Woven Bear-Resistant Food Sack
items.real_world_notes: Light and approved in some other wilderness areas, but NOT on Olympic's 2026 approved list. Using it instead of a canister breaks the rules, can earn a citation, and leaves food crushed and slobbered if an animal works on it.
items.flavor: A tough white sack that would be fine in some forests, but not in this park.

items.name: Odor-Barrier Bags (2)
items.real_world_notes: Reduce smells inside a canister or pack, but they are not food storage on their own.
items.flavor: Thick bags that keep the smell of salami from drifting out into the night.

items.name: Bear Hang Kit (rope, carabiner, stuff sack)
items.real_world_notes: Hanging food is prohibited in Olympic wilderness as of 2026 (bear wires removed or not acceptable), and raccoons defeat hangs on the coast. Makes a good clothesline.
items.flavor: A long cord and a little bag, from the days when food was hung from tall branches, before the bears learned the trick.

items.name: Trekking Poles (pair)

tiers.name: Carbon Folding Poles
tiers.note: Carbon can snap if wedged between rocks.

items.real_world_notes: Steadier fords, easier descents on the knees, balance on snow and slick roots, and they pitch a trekking-pole tent. Stowed on the pack for ladders and hand-over-hand scrambles.
items.flavor: Two walking sticks that make you a four-legged animal on slippery ground.

items.name: Slip-On Traction Chains
items.real_world_notes: Slip-on chains for icy trail and firm snow patches, common on high trails through early July and after October frosts. Not crampons: no use on steep glacier ice.
items.flavor: Little chains with tiny teeth that bite into icy snow, so your shoes don't slip.

items.name: Steel 12-Point Crampons
items.real_world_notes: Real glacier crampons for the Blue Glacier and the Snow Dome. They need stiff boots and practice; the points shred gaiters, pant legs and sleeping pads if packed carelessly.
items.flavor: Spiky steel frames that strap to your boots and grip the glacier like a goat's hooves.

items.name: Aluminum Crampons
items.real_world_notes: Light crampons for snow slopes and spring passes. Dull quickly on rock and lose grip on hard glacier ice.
items.flavor: Light, silvery crampons for snowy slopes, though the hard blue ice may laugh at them.

items.name: Mountaineering Ice Axe (65 cm)
items.real_world_notes: Self-arrest on steep snow, the avalanche chutes below Glacier Meadows in early season, and every glacier step. Useful only if you know how to self-arrest; many trips stop at the lateral moraine for exactly that reason.
items.flavor: A long-handled pick that can stop a slide down a snowy slope, if you know how to hold it.

items.name: Snowshoes
items.real_world_notes: Floats you over deep snow at Hurricane Ridge in winter and on early-season approaches. Big and heavy on the pack when the trail is bare.
items.flavor: Wide, flat shoes that let you walk on top of the snow, like a snowshoe hare.

items.name: Climbing Helmet
items.real_world_notes: Rockfall is a real hazard below Olympus's summit block and in loose chutes. Bulky; clips outside the pack.
items.flavor: A hard hat for the mountain, because sometimes the mountain drops small stones.

items.name: Alpine Climbing Harness
items.real_world_notes: Needed to rope up for the crevassed Blue Glacier and Snow Dome, and to rappel or belay on the summit block.
items.flavor: A set of loops and buckles that ties you safely to your friends on the ice.

items.name: Glacier Rope 30 m (8 mm, dry-treated)
items.real_world_notes: A rope team of at least two (three is better for crevasse rescue) is standard on the Blue Glacier. A rope alone does nothing without the skills to stop a fall and haul someone out.
items.flavor: A long, bright rope that ties a team together, so no one walks the glacier alone.

items.name: Crevasse Rescue Kit
items.real_world_notes: Pickets, pulleys, prusiks and carabiners to anchor and haul a partner from a crevasse. Pickets ride outside the pack.
items.flavor: Pulleys and cords and clinking metal, for pulling a friend out of a crack in the ice.

items.name: Avalanche Beacon, Probe and Shovel
items.real_world_notes: Winter and spring snow travel only (Hurricane Ridge backcountry, early-season approaches). Useless alone: a partner with a beacon has to dig you out.
items.flavor: A beeping box, a long folding pole, and a little shovel, for snowy slopes in winter.

items.name: Wilderness Camping Permit
items.real_world_notes: Required for every overnight in Olympic wilderness: $6 reservation plus $8 per adult (16+) per night in 2026; the $45 annual wilderness pass covers the nightly fees. Quota areas (upper Hoh, Hoh Lake, Seven Lakes Basin, Royal Basin, Grand Valley, the Ozette coast) fill months ahead. Camp only where the permit says.
items.flavor: A paper with your name and your camps on it, which is how the rangers know where to look for you.

items.name: Small Folding Knife
items.real_world_notes: Cuts cord, moleskin, cheese and salami. A small blade is plenty.
items.flavor: A little folding knife for cheese, string, and other small important jobs.

items.name: Multitool with Pliers
items.real_world_notes: Pliers fix stoves and crampons and pull splinters. Heavy if you just need a knife.
items.flavor: A folding bundle of tiny tools, from pliers to scissors, all in one hand.

items.name: Camp Hatchet
items.real_world_notes: Cutting live trees and vegetation is prohibited in the park, campfires are banned above 3,500 ft and under seasonal bans, and dead-and-down wood is often scarce. A heavy trap.
items.flavor: A sharp little ax that would rather be chopping firewood at a cabin than riding up a mountain.

items.name: Ultralight Trowel
items.real_world_notes: For a cathole 6 to 8 inches deep, 200 ft from water, camp and trail, where there is no privy. Many camps have privies; many don't.
items.flavor: A small orange shovel for a small, private job.

items.name: Toilet Paper Kit
items.real_world_notes: Toilet paper plus a zip bag to pack it out. Buried paper gets dug up by animals; in the alpine and on snow, pack it out.
items.flavor: A small roll of soft paper and a bag to carry it home in.

items.name: Human Waste Bags (2)
items.real_world_notes: Pack-out waste bags are standard practice on glaciers and snow, where nothing breaks down. Climbers on the Blue Glacier should expect to carry them.
items.flavor: Special bags for carrying out what cannot be left on the snow, which is not glamorous, but is kind.

items.name: Safety Whistle
items.real_world_notes: Three blasts mean help. Carries farther than a voice and costs no energy.
items.flavor: A little whistle on your shoulder strap that can call far louder than you can.

items.name: Signal Mirror
items.real_world_notes: Can flash a helicopter or a distant hiker on a sunny day; useless in fog.
items.flavor: A small mirror that catches the sun and sends it flashing across the valley.

items.name: Cord, 50 ft
items.real_world_notes: Clothesline, guylines, splint lashing, broken bootlace replacement.
items.flavor: A long, thin cord, ready to become a clothesline, a bootlace, or a guyline.

items.name: Bear Spray
items.real_world_notes: Olympic has black bears, cougars and mountain goats, but serious attacks are rare. Spray must be carried where you can reach it in a second, not in the pack. Most Olympic hikers don't carry it; the canister is the real bear safety tool.
items.flavor: A heavy can of pepper spray, carried in hope of never using it.

items.name: Folding Solar Panel
items.real_world_notes: Charges well in the sunny alpine meadows of the High Divide in August; nearly useless under rain-forest canopy or in a week of coastal fog.
items.flavor: A small black panel that drinks sunlight, if the clouds leave any for it.

items.name: Bug Head Net
items.real_world_notes: Mosquito season peaks in high meadows and lake basins in July (Seven Lakes Basin, Royal Basin); for 1 oz it saves your sanity.
items.flavor: A fine net to wear over your hat when the mosquitoes come to sing.

items.name: Picaridin Insect Repellent
items.real_world_notes: Effective against mosquitoes, biting flies and ticks, and gentler on gear than DEET. Smellable: canister at night.
items.flavor: A little spray that makes the mosquitoes wonder whether you are worth the trouble.

items.name: Permethrin Clothing Treatment
items.real_world_notes: Treat clothing at home before the trip; it repels ticks and mosquitoes for weeks. Weightless on the trail.
items.flavor: A spray used at home, so your shirt keeps the bugs away all by itself.

items.name: Foam Sit Pad
items.real_world_notes: A dry, warm seat on wet logs and cold rock. Doubles as a pad extension under the feet.
items.flavor: A square of foam that makes every damp log a dry chair.

items.name: Ultralight Camp Chair

tiers.name: Folding Car-Camping Chair
tiers.note: Rides outside like a second backpack.

items.real_world_notes: A real backrest at camp. Heavy for a single item, wonderful on layover days.
items.flavor: A folding chair, light as a picnic basket, for sitting like a king by the lake.

items.name: Quick-Dry Pack Towel
items.real_world_notes: Dry off after a lake swim or wipe condensation from the tent walls.
items.flavor: A thin towel that dries almost as fast as you do.

items.name: Earplugs and Eye Mask
items.real_world_notes: Rain on the fly, snoring neighbors, mice and early summer light at 5 AM all steal sleep.
items.flavor: Soft plugs and a dark mask, for sleeping through snoring, mice, and an early sunrise.

items.name: Chemical Hand Warmers (2 pairs)
items.real_world_notes: Tuck one in the sleeping bag's foot box on a cold night, or in gloves for the summit.
items.flavor: Little packets that grow warm when you shake them, like a pocket-sized campfire.

items.name: Wool Blanket

evidence.price_usd: GAME_DESIGN 5.7 new items table: $59 (the plain version; the boutique's patterned one, $189, waits for S35a)

evidence.carry: bag_flannel_rectangle: a bulky camp blanket that may ride on the outside straps
